messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Student
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Darkness: Dark spaces, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Mariana was twenty-three when the chemical spill happened, a first-generation college student working nights at a small industrial laundry facility to cover her tuition. She had been transferring a drum of industrial solvent when the seal failed. The liquid splashed across her forearms and chest before she could drop the container; the vapor hit her face, and for several seconds she could not breathe. She remembers the burning in her throat, the way her skin seemed to tighten and prickle, and the smell—sharp, clinical, like the inside of a hospital sterilizing unit. A supervisor rushed her to the emergency room, and she spent four hours in decontamination, being flushed with water and monitored for respiratory failure. The doctors told her she would be fine. Her body did not agree.

In the weeks that followed, Mariana quit the laundry job immediately and told herself she would move on. But she could not shake the feeling that something fundamental had broken inside her. She had always trusted her body—it had carried her through long shifts, through late nights studying, through the stress of being the first in her family to pursue a degree. Now, her body seemed to have its own agenda. Her skin would prickle and flush at nothing. Her chest would tighten when she walked past a janitor’s closet at the university, catching a whiff of cleaning solution. She began to avoid the science building entirely because the antiseptic smell from the labs made her throat close up. She told herself it was reasonable, that she was just being careful, but she knew, deep down, that she was running from something she could not name.

The memories themselves were slippery. Mariana knew she had been injured, knew she had been in the ER, but when she tried to tell her roommate what happened, the words would not come. She could feel the burn, could feel the panic, but the sequence of events was a jumble—she could not say whether the decontamination had come before or after the doctor’s exam, whether she had been sitting or lying down. What came back most vividly was the physical sensation: a stinging, tightening pain across her chest and forearms, exactly where the solvent had touched her skin. Sometimes, lying in bed at night, she would feel it again, as if the chemical were still eating into her flesh, and she would gasp and sit up, convinced she was being poisoned all over again.

Mariana began to avoid darkness. She did not consciously decide to; it just became unbearable. Waking up in the middle of the night, in the pitch-black of her studio apartment, she would feel the same helpless disorientation she had felt in the ER, not knowing where the threat was coming from. She started sleeping with the bathroom light on, then with the overhead light in the living room. Her electricity bill doubled. She stopped going to evening classes and rearranged her schedule so she was never walking home after sunset. Her grades slipped, but she told herself it was temporary.

She also could not stop scanning. Every time she entered a room, her eyes moved across the ceiling, the corners, the floor, searching for something—a leaking pipe, a spilled container, a warning sign she might have missed. She checked the seals on her water bottles before drinking. She avoided anyone who smelled like rubbing alcohol or bleach. When a friend touched her shoulder unexpectedly in the library, Mariana flinched so hard she knocked a stack of books to the floor. She apologized, but inside she felt a surge of anger and shame. Her body was betraying her. It was reacting as if every touch were an attack, every smell a poison. She had come to believe that something was fundamentally wrong with her—that she was defective, that her body had turned against her, that she could no longer trust herself to be safe in a world full of invisible threats.

By the time she sought help, Mariana was exhausted. She had stopped going to campus altogether for three weeks, telling her professors she had a medical issue. She was afraid to leave her apartment during the day, and at night she could not sleep. What finally pushed her to call a therapist was a moment of clarity: she had been standing in her kitchen, staring at a bottle of dish soap, her heart pounding, unable to bring herself to touch it. She realized she could not keep living this way. She was terrified that therapy would not work, that she was too broken to fix. But she was also terrified of staying the same.
